name: David Baker

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on a timber-frame crew for Northfold Homes. The wall panels get made in their factory, come out on a lorry, and we crane them into place and fix them together, so a house goes from slab to roof in about a week. I'm the junior, so I'm on the tag lines, nailing off sole plates, fetching fixings and getting shouted at by Gav (our crew leader) when I'm slow. I love the speed of it, though, watching a whole street appear in a month.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What came before this, and what's home like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I left school at fifteen, did a few years driving delivery vans, then got sick of being told where to go by a handset. I've been on the frames for about eighteen months, and I've got my basic trade certificate. I share a terraced house with two mates and I've got about four months' money saved. I use AI every day: I photograph the panel drawings and get it to talk me through them, and I'm teaching myself basic electronics with it in the evenings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably be the one saying it's a shame, to be honest. Everyone on the crew would laugh at me, because Gav already thinks I'm on my phone too much. I'd say it's still a good tool, just not magic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, not much changes, which is fine. Northfold's got a full order book for two years and the timber-frame side is growing. I'd still be a junior learning the trade, just with a handy helper on my phone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going on the frames and push to get on the crane signalling course this spring, because it pays more. I'd keep using AI for the drawings and the evening learning. And I'd keep the four months' savings where they are.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, really. A bit flat, maybe, because I was looking forward to the interesting version.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd lose if AI turns out to be mostly hype?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The evenings, probably. I've learned more about wiring from a chatbot at my kitchen table than I learned in four years of school. If AI stays a bit rubbish, that's still worth having.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's your money situation like if Northfold has a quiet patch?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Four months covers it. We get rained off sometimes and lose a day's pay, and in January there's a slow week or two. I'd pick up delivery driving shifts again if it got really bad.

say: I'd say it's **a shame**, and the crew would laugh at me for it.
I'd say AI is still **a good tool**, just not magic.
think: Northfold has a **full order book** for two years, so little changes for me.
I'd still be a **junior learning** the trade with a handy helper.
do: Book the **crane signalling course** this spring for the higher pay.
Keep using AI for **panel drawings** and evening study.
Keep the **four months** of savings untouched.
feel: He feels **calm**, and a little **flat** about missing the interesting version.
S0.quote: I've learned more about wiring from a chatbot at my kitchen table than I learned in four years of school.
fieldNote: He is the rare worker who'd be **disappointed** by AI fizzling out.
His job looks secure because of Northfold's **two-year order book**.
His fallback is **delivery driving**, which he's done before.

steps.text: Book the crane signalling course this spring for better pay
Keep studying basic electronics with a chatbot in the evenings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is good if the gains get shared. If it saves the firm a fortune, the people on site should see some of that in pay and shorter weeks. I'd post that, and I'd probably get into an argument with my uncle about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think it's good for me. My job's hands-on, so the robots come slowly, and meanwhile the thinking bits of construction, the planning and ordering, get done by software that I already know how to use. A junior who can work the tablet and the crane is worth more than one who can't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Northfold if I could help trial whatever software they bring in for site plans and deliveries. I'd finish an electrical basics course at college by next autumn. And I'd keep saving, maybe fifty quid a week more, so I'm free to jump to a better job if one comes up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty good, actually. Excited, with a small voice saying don't get cocky.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on your crew would struggle with this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Gav, definitely. My crew leader Gav can read a frame by eye but won't touch the site tablet, and the office keeps sending Gav things on it. I'd want to help him, not show him up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd be learning electronics. Where's that actually heading?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fixing and running the machines. If robots start showing up on frame sites, someone needs to set them out, maintain them and fix the sensors. I'd rather be that person than the one being replaced.

say: I'd say this is good **if the gains** are shared with people on site.
I'd argue for **better pay** and shorter weeks when firms save money.
think: My job is **hands-on**, so robots arrive slowly while software takes the planning.
A junior who can work **the tablet and crane** becomes worth more.
do: Ask Northfold to **trial the new software** for site plans and deliveries.
Finish an **electrical basics** course at college by next autumn.
Save an extra **fifty a week** to stay free to switch jobs.
feel: He feels **excited**, with a small voice warning him not to get cocky.

fieldNote: He sees the **thinking side** of construction changing first and positions himself there.
His progressive view shows up as **sharing gains**, not stopping the change.
He's protective of **Gav**, an older leader who avoids the tablet.

steps.text: Volunteer to trial Northfold's new site planning software
Finish an electrical basics course at college by next autumn
Put an extra fifty a week into savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need a plan for everybody, not just tech people. Stuff like a guaranteed income while people retrain, and the robot firms paying for it. I'd go to protests about that, which I've never done before.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it's a lot closer than I'd like. In 2028 the software can design and plan the whole house, so Northfold needs fewer office people but still needs us. Then in 2031 robots can crane and fix panels, and a junior like me is exactly what they'd replace first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go hard on the electronics and try to get a job with a robotics firm or the people who service site machines before 2031. I'd save everything I can and stop going out on Fridays. I'd also sign up to whatever union covers construction, because I've never bothered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous, a bit sick. I'm still curious, but curious from further back than I'd like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Five months ago you were looking forward to this. Has that changed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah, it's changed. Looking forward to the robots is easy when the robots are ten years away, not three. I still think I can get on the right side of it, but two years isn't long to learn a whole new trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to your housemates and your rent in that picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: One mate does customer service for an energy firm, and that's gone by 2028, probably. The other's a chef. So the rent might land on two of us or me, and that's when the four months starts disappearing fast.

say: I'd say we need **a plan for everybody**, not just tech people.
I'd join protests for a **guaranteed income** while people retrain.
think: By **2031** robots could crane and fix panels, and juniors go first.
Two years is **not long** to learn a whole new trade.
do: Study electronics hard to join a **robot servicing** firm before 2031.
Stop **Friday nights out** and save everything possible.
Join a **construction union** for the first time.
feel: He feels **nervous** and a bit sick, still curious but from further back.
S2.quote: Looking forward to the robots is easy when the robots are ten years away, not three.
fieldNote: His enthusiasm **flips to nerves** once the timeline is short.
He sees the **three-year gap** as just enough time to switch, if he moves fast.
His rent depends on a housemate in **customer service**, exposed in 2028.

steps.text: Apply to firms that service site robots before 2031
Study electronics every evening to reach technician level
Stop Friday nights out and save every spare pound
Join a construction union and go to its protests

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the time for big public training schemes, and for the firms to put money in. I'd post about it but less angrily. Five years means people can still be organised about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I'd make it. Five years gets me through an electrical apprenticeship or a robotics technician course. By 2034 I'd want to be the person who sets up and repairs the frame robots, not the one holding the tag line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start a part-time technician course next September, three evenings a week. I'd talk to Northfold about whether they'd sponsor it. And I'd keep the savings growing towards six months, so I could take a pay cut for a year if a good training job came up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy, but mostly focused. Like having a hard exam on a date you know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does five years let you do that two didn't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Time to qualify, basically. Two years is a crash course, but five years is an actual trade with a certificate at the end. And I'd have a few more years of savings in the bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If you could tell Northfold one thing, what would it be?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Train your own people for the robots now. They'll need folk who know what a frame is supposed to look like when it's right. Better that's us than some contractor flown in from somewhere.

say: I'd say this is the time for **public training schemes** funded by the firms.
Five years means people can still **organise** around it.
think: Five years gets me through a **technician course** before robots arrive in 2034.
I'd want to **repair the frame robots**, not hold the tag line.
do: Start a part-time **technician course** next September, three evenings a week.
Grow savings toward **six months** to afford a training pay cut.
feel: He feels a bit **uneasy** but mostly **focused**, like facing a dated exam.
S3.quote: Two years is a crash course, but five years is an actual trade with a certificate at the end.
fieldNote: The extra years turn panic into a **study plan** with dates.
He wants Northfold to **train its own** staff for the robots.
Savings become a tool for a **pay cut** while training, not just a buffer.

steps.text: Start a part-time technician course next September

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift if we use it. I'd want the government to make every construction apprenticeship include the machines. I'd be fairly upbeat about it in public.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think it suits me well. I'd have years on the frames to really learn building, then move into the tech side when it matters. Robots on site around 2039 means I'd be in my forties with skills nobody else has.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year, nothing dramatic. I'd keep going on the frames, do the crane course and start the electronics evening classes. Maybe in a few years I'd look at a small business doing site surveys with drones and scanners.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and quite excited, really. It's the version where I get to be good at two things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd be thirty-seven by 2036. Where would you want to be?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By thirty-seven I want to be the bloke Northfold rings when the frame robot goes wrong on a wet Tuesday. Good pay, my own van, maybe a flat I own instead of renting with mates.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about ten years that worries you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I'd get lazy. Ten years feels like ages, and I could easily spend five of them just nailing panels and saying I'll start next year.

say: I'd say ten years is **a gift** if we use it.
I'd want every apprenticeship to **include the machines**.
think: I'd get years on the frames to **really learn building** first.
With robots around **2039**, I'd be in my forties with rare skills.

feel: He feels **calm and excited**, seeing a chance to be good at two things.

steps.text: Take the crane signalling course on the frames this year

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, AGI by 2028. I like the tech, but two years isn't enough to retrain, and my rent depends on a mate whose job goes first. What would help is a paid training place, where you get a wage while you learn the robot side.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe how much the juniors know. People think the new lads are just muscle, but half of us are the ones teaching the old boys how to use the site tablet. We could be useful in this if anyone asked.

headlineQuote: People think the new lads are just muscle, but half of us are the ones teaching the old boys how to use the site tablet.
portrait: David is a 27-year-old **junior** on a **timber-frame crew**, after years driving delivery vans.
He uses AI **every day** to read drawings and teach himself electronics.
He's **progressive**, wanting the gains shared through pay, shorter weeks and training.
He's calm in slow scenarios but **anxious** with AGI by 2028, when retraining time runs short.
With **ten years**, he plans to become the technician who fixes the frame robots.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because two years is too short to retrain and his rent depends on exposed housemates.
